title: A Clinic at the Entrance to Heliópolis, and One That Had to Close
dek: In 2011 Thomaz Srougi opened low-price private clinics for São Paulo's uninsured; one closed for lack of patients, and he spent three years making the other work.

story.event: Opening a low-price private clinic at the entrance to the Heliópolis favela and testing the model for three years
story.summary: In August 2011 Thomaz Srougi opened a Dr. Consulta clinic at the entrance to Heliópolis in São Paulo, charging low fixed prices to uninsured patients and accepting no health plans; a smaller trial clinic in São Mateus closed after nine months for lack of patients. He spent about three years proving the Heliópolis clinic despite low awareness and repeated robberies, then expanded from 2014 with venture funding, reaching 45 clinics by 2017.
paragraphs: In August 2011 a small private clinic opened at the entrance to Heliópolis, São Paulo's largest favela, between a bank branch and a department store. It accepted no health insurance and no card from SUS, the public health system. A sign by the gate gave the prices plainly: 40 reais for a general practitioner, 60 for any of ten specialties, payable in two instalments. About a dozen doctors worked there, all also attached to leading hospitals such as Sírio-Libanês and Albert Einstein. The clinic's founder, Thomaz Srougi, was not a doctor.

His father, Miguel Srougi, was one of Brazil's best-known urologists; Thomaz had trained in business, worked in finance at the brewer Ambev and, from 2007 to 2011, run an investment fund with former colleagues. While studying management at Harvard he had noticed Mexico's Farmacias Similares, which offered cheap consultations beside their pharmacies, and thought a low-price network could be profitable and do Brazil good. He knew millions of people had no health plan and were tired of public queues. He did not know whether they would pay.

He tested it twice. A smaller clinic in São Mateus, in the east of the city, was meant as a trial; Veja São Paulo later reported that it closed after nine months for lack of patients. At first, Srougi said, nobody understood the model. He handed out leaflets outside hospitals and asked evangelical churches for a chance to announce the service. A survey he commissioned found that only one in ten of the 300,000 people around Heliópolis knew the clinic existed, and after about 1 million reais spent on fitting it out, it was not yet covering its costs. To stretch the money he drew the logo himself in PowerPoint, and a door, handle still on, served as a desk. The clinic was robbed six times, with doctors held at gunpoint.

He stayed in Heliópolis for three years. Only in 2014, after that testing phase, did the company begin to expand, helped by about 30 million reais from the funds Kaszek Ventures and LGTVP. Early on, he said that year, he had lost sleep over not having the money for the bills; now it was the duty to honour other people's money. By October 2017 there were 45 clinics.

quote.text: He who adds to what he has, will keep off bright-eyed hunger; for if you add only a little to a little and do this often, soon that little will become great.
quote.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg eBook #348
quote.connection: Hesiod was advising a farmer on keeping hunger from the door, not a founder on growth. His point still fits a clinic that had to be explained leaflet by leaflet: small additions, made often, are how a little becomes enough. Srougi's three years in Heliópolis were built from exactly such additions.

reflection: Srougi ran two trials at once and let one of them end. São Mateus was meant as a test, and when patients did not come it closed. Heliópolis, robbed and barely known, stayed open for three years before anyone put serious money behind it. One in ten people knowing you exist is a poor figure, and it is also a starting one.

You may be in a stretch where few people understand what you are making, or why. Hesiod's advice is unglamorous and kind: add a little, and do it often. One leaflet, one conversation, one more person who now knows you exist. None of that needs to happen in a rush, and none of it is wasted.
invitation: Tell one person who does not yet know about your work what it does, in two sentences. Then ask them one question about what they would need from it, and write down the answer.

cross_checks.claim: Dr. Consulta's clinic at the entrance to Heliópolis opened in 2011 (August, per Saúde Business), founded by Thomaz Srougi
The clinics charged low fixed prices, took no health plans and used doctors from leading São Paulo hospitals
A second 2011 clinic in São Mateus opened and later closed
Srougi spent about three years in Heliópolis before expansion began in 2014
Srougi is the son of the urologist Miguel Srougi and came from business and finance, including Ambev

research_notes: All of Srougi's own words in the sources are in Portuguese, so the story reports them in paraphrase rather than as translated quotations: 'No começo, ninguém entendia nosso modelo de atuação' (at first nobody understood the model), and 'Se no começo eu perdia o sono por não ter recursos para as contas, hoje não durmo pela responsabilidade de honrar o dinheiro dos outros' (Veja São Paulo, 2014). First clinic: the slate and most sources say Heliópolis; a 2017 brandchannel interview (reposted on a personal blog, not cited) says the first clinic was in São Mateus. Veja São Paulo says both opened in 2011, and Portuguese Wikipedia says São Mateus closed in 2011 while Veja says it closed after nine months; the story says only that it was a trial that closed after nine months, attributed to Veja. The Saúde Business page is dated 24 July 2012 but may republish an earlier article; it says the clinic opened in August 2011 and 'today' does 600 procedures a month, so the story avoids giving that figure a date. Money: Saúde Business reports about R$1 million invested in the structure; Veja (2014) implies about R$3 million over the first three years (2014 revenue of R$6 million being 'double the investment'); the story uses the earlier, narrower figure for fitting out the clinic. Funding is set to 'mixed' rather than the slate's 'venture': the first three years were paid for by Srougi and his partners (Portuguese Wikipedia names the investment firm Galicia Investimentos, which no other source here confirms, so it is not used), and venture money arrived in 2014. Background: Veja says he was a partner in the builder Tenda; Estadão says he worked at Gafisa (which acquired Tenda in 2008); neither is used. The Hesiod line comes from the passage on giving and saving that Evelyn-White's prose translation heads ll. 352-369; the locator gives that range because the translation does not number individual lines.
